title: The gap in the coal
teaches: How fungi rot wood, white rot and brown rot, and whether the late arrival of lignin-breaking fungi explains the age of coal
summary: **Wood is three materials.** Cellulose fibres, hemicellulose between them, and lignin, a tough glue that few living things can break.
**White rot fungi break all three.** They use enzymes that make reactive molecules to tear lignin apart, and leave the wood pale and stringy.
**Brown rot fungi take the sugars and leave the lignin.** The wood turns brown, shrinks and cracks into cubes.
**Brown rot evolved from white rot several times.** Its fungi lost most of the lignin-breaking genes and attack cellulose with iron chemistry instead.
**Much of the world's coal formed in the Carboniferous, about 359 to 299 million years ago.** Coal is buried plant matter that never rotted.
**Floudas and colleagues dated lignin-breaking enzymes to about the end of the Carboniferous.** In 2012 they proposed that coal piled up because nothing could yet rot lignin.

**Nelsen and colleagues answered that wet ground made the coal.** In 2016 they showed that coal follows wet, sinking lowlands, that the coal-age trees were mostly bark, and that coal kept forming after white rot arose.
**Wood-rotting fungi return most of a forest's dead wood to the air as carbon dioxide.** The lignin left by brown rot can stay in the soil for centuries.

blocks.text: Coal is plant matter that was buried before it could rot, squeezed and heated under kilometres of rock until little was left but carbon. It has formed at many times in the Earth's history, but not evenly. A large share of the world's black coal was laid down in one stretch of about sixty million years, from about 359 to 299 million years ago. Geologists named that stretch the **Carboniferous**, the coal-bearing period, after the coal seams of Britain.

The forests that made it were strange. The tallest trees were giant clubmosses thirty metres high, with trunks patterned like snakeskin, beside tree ferns and horsetails the size of trees. They grew in vast lowland swamps near the equator. When they fell, many of them never rotted. Why so much wood failed to rot then, and so much less of it since, is a question this lesson takes from two sides. It starts with how wood rots now.

Lesson 3 met cellulose, a long chain of glucose, and lignin, which wraps it. A piece of wood is three materials together. **Cellulose** makes up nearly half: bundles of chains laid side by side into fibres, very strong for their weight. **Hemicellulose**, shorter and branched chains of several sugars, fills about a quarter and binds the fibres to each other. **Lignin**, about a quarter to a third, fills every remaining gap and sets hard.

Lignin is what lets a tree stand. It stiffens the cell walls so that a trunk can hold up a crown, and it waterproofs the tubes that carry water up from the roots. It is also a fortress. Cellulose is a chain of one repeated unit, so an enzyme shaped to fit one link fits them all. Lignin has no repeated unit. Its building blocks are joined irregularly, in many different ways, so there is no single link for an enzyme to fit, and it shields the cellulose underneath. Most bacteria and almost all animals cannot eat wood at all; the termites and beetles that do rely on microbes or fungi to help them.[^termites]

Most of the fungi that rot standing and fallen wood are club fungi, the group of the mushrooms and brackets. They do it in two ways, and anyone who breaks open old logs in a forest can tell the two apart.

**White rot** fungi eat all three parts of the wood. With no link for an enzyme to fit, they do not cut lignin directly. Instead they release enzymes, called peroxidases, that make small, highly reactive molecules, and these tear at whatever lignin they touch, breaking it into pieces the fungus can take in. Lignin is what makes wood brown, so a log rotted this way turns pale, then soft, stringy or spongy, until it can be pulled apart in wet white strands. The turkey tail and the oyster mushroom are white rot fungi, and so are most of the brackets on broadleaf trees.[^spalting]

**Brown rot** fungi take the cellulose and hemicellulose and leave the lignin. They release small molecules that gather iron from the wood and make hydrogen peroxide, and the two react to make the hydroxyl radical, a molecule so reactive that it breaks cellulose chains wherever it forms. That opens the wood first; the fungus's own enzymes then digest the broken chains.[^fenton] The lignin is left, slightly altered. With its fibres gone the wood darkens, shrinks and cracks across and along the grain into brown cubes that crumble to powder between the fingers. Brown rot is commonest on the wood of conifers. The dry rot that destroys timber in damp houses is a brown rot.

blocks.text: When the genomes of wood-rotting fungi were read, they showed which way round the two had evolved. White rot is the older way. Brown rot fungi descend from white rot ancestors, and have lost most of the genes for lignin-breaking peroxidases. The loss happened several separate times, in separate lineages. Without the peroxidases, brown rot fungi cannot eat the lignin, but they still reach the sugars, and they rot wood fast.

In 2012 a team of more than seventy scientists, led by Dimitrios Floudas and David Hibbett of Clark University in Massachusetts, compared the genomes of 31 fungi. They traced the family of lignin-breaking peroxidase genes back through the fungal family tree and estimated when it first appeared, by assuming that genes change at a roughly steady rate.[^clock] Their answer was about 295 million years ago, just after the end of the Carboniferous; with the wide uncertainty of such dates, it could have been somewhat earlier or later.

They suggested what that might mean. Before white rot, little could break lignin, so on their view lignin from fallen trees would have piled up and been buried. Once fungi learned to break it, wood rotted away, and coal formation fell. The idea was simple and widely reported: the coal age was the age before wood could rot.

Four years later Matthew Nelsen, with the palaeobotanists William DiMichele and Kevin Boyce and the geologist Shanan Peters, tested the idea against the coal itself. Their paper's title gave their verdict: *Delayed fungal evolution did not cause the Paleozoic peak in coal production*. They made three points.

First, the coal-forming trees were not especially woody. The giant clubmosses were mostly thick bark around a thin core of wood, so much of their bulk was not lignin-rich wood at all. Second, coal did not fall away when the peroxidases arrived. Coal kept forming in the Permian, the period that followed, from 299 to 252 million years ago, and thick seams have formed since wherever conditions allowed, including the soft brown coals of the last few tens of millions of years. Third, the peak of Carboniferous coal matches the geography. As the continents crowded together into the supercontinent Pangaea, wide, sinking lowlands formed along the young mountain belts, right in the wet tropics. Water stood on them year round.

Waterlogged ground is a place where almost nothing rots, fungus or not. A fungus breathes oxygen, and in a swamp the oxygen in the water is used up within centimetres of the surface. Wood that falls into it is preserved as peat, the first step to coal. Nelsen's group argued that the coal came from a world with an unusual amount of swamp, kept wet and sinking for millions of years, and that the fungi were beside the point.

blocks.text: Neither side disputes the rough date of the genes, or the lack of oxygen in swamps. What they disagree on is which mattered more for the coal. Nelsen's group granted that the arrival of white rot did change how fast wood on dry ground returns to the air.[^since]

Wood is the largest store of carbon above ground in a forest. When a tree dies, the fungi that rot it turn most of that carbon back into carbon dioxide over years to decades, by breathing out what they digest. Without them, far more of that carbon would stay locked in fallen trunks instead of returning to the air for new plants to use. A forest's dead wood is part of the carbon cycle mainly because fungi can eat it.

Brown rot leaves something behind. Its brown, lignin-rich crumbs resist further decay and can stay in the soil for centuries, darkening it and holding water like a sponge. In northern conifer forests, where brown rot is common, such remains are a part of the dark layer under the needles. So a rotting log is turned by fungi partly into air and partly into soil.

blocks.caption: Five questions on rot and coal
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What makes lignin so hard to digest?
choices: It has no single repeating link for an enzyme to fit
It is made of glucose joined very tightly
items.why: Cellulose repeats one unit, so an enzyme that fits one link fits all. Lignin's pieces are joined irregularly, so white rot fungi break it with reactive molecules that their enzymes make.

items.ask: An old log is pale, soft and comes apart in white strands. Which kind of rot is it?
choices: White rot, which has broken down the lignin too
Brown rot, which has broken down the lignin
No rot: the wood was always pale
items.why: Lignin is what makes wood brown. White rot removes it with the cellulose, leaving pale strands.

items.ask: How did brown rot fungi arise?
choices: From white rot ancestors that lost most of their lignin-breaking genes
From bacteria that live in wood
Before white rot, as the first wood-eaters
items.why: Genomes show brown rot evolved from white rot several separate times, each time losing peroxidase genes.

items.ask: What did Floudas and colleagues propose in 2012?
choices: Coal piled up because no fungus could yet break lignin
Fungi made coal by eating wood
items.why: They dated lignin-breaking peroxidases to about 295 million years ago, around the end of the coal age, and suggested the timing was not chance.

items.ask: Why did Nelsen and colleagues think swamps mattered more than fungi?
choices: Wood in waterlogged ground barely rots, and coal follows the wet basins of the time
Swamps are full of white rot fungi
items.why: Fungi need oxygen, and waterlogged ground has almost none. Coal matched the wide, sinking, wet lowlands of the Carboniferous, and kept forming after white rot arose.

termites.title: Who else eats wood
termites.text: Termites digest wood with the help of microbes in their guts, and some termites farm a fungus, *Termitomyces*, on chewed plant matter in their nests and eat the fungus. Many wood-boring beetle larvae rely on fungi that have already softened the wood. A few bacteria can break some lignin, but slowly.

spalting.title: Spalted wood
spalting.text: Where two white rot fungi meet inside a log, each walls itself off with a dark line of pigment. Woodworkers prize the result, spalted wood, for its black lines wandering across pale grain, and some grow it on purpose by inoculating blocks.

fenton.title: Iron chemistry
fenton.text: Iron and hydrogen peroxide react to make the hydroxyl radical, one of the most reactive molecules known. The reaction was found by Henry Fenton in 1894 and bears his name. Brown rot fungi seem to make it a little way from their hyphae, so that it does not damage the fungus itself.

clock.title: A molecular clock
clock.text: Genes pick up changes over time. If the rate is roughly known, the number of differences between two gene versions gives the time since they split. The rate is checked against fossils of known age, and the dates carry wide error bars: tens of millions of years either way.

since.title: Where wood still piles up
since.text: On dry ground today, most of the carbon in small fallen wood returns to the air within decades, though big logs can take a century or more. Only in waterlogged places, such as peat bogs, does dead plant matter still pile up for thousands of years, which is why peatlands, on a few per cent of the land, hold a large share of the world's soil carbon.
